content.text: Part A: Read Craft Images Closely (RI.6.7)
(15 minutes)
Think-Pair-Share
Directions:

Work with your partner to analyze one of the craft images using the Media Literacy Image Analysis organizer. Record exact details from the image, then explain what those details suggest about skill, culture, or value. Finally, add one note about how the image adds to what we have already learned from
A Single Shard
about observation, practice, or apprenticeship.
Which details does the image include and emphasize? What connections can you make to what you already know about observation, practice, or apprenticeship from reading
A Single Shard
? What does the image omit, and why does that omission matter?
Part B: Select a Visual Source to Carry Forward (W.6.8)
(15 minutes)
Quick Write
Directions:

Choose one visual source connected to Korean art, pottery, or craft traditions that you want to study more closely in the next lesson. In 2–3 sentences, identify what the image includes, what it seems to emphasize or omit, and why it is a useful source for your research notes.
Which visual source did you choose, and why is it worth carrying forward into the next lesson?
What is one note you will want to remember when you return to this image in the next lesson?
Pulse Check
Which response is the best example of a strong visual source analysis statement?
A. This picture is pretty, so it is a good source.
B. The image has pottery in it, and pottery is important in the book.
C. The image centers the unfinished bowl and the potter’s hands, so it highlights the process of making and helps me understand the practice behind the finished art.
D. The image was taken a long time ago, so it must show exactly what Tree-ear saw.
Quick Write
Directions:
Use your notes from today to answer both reflection prompts. Be specific about one visual choice you noticed and one next step you will take as a researcher.
What new information did you learn today from a visual source that words alone did not make as clear?
What is your next step for the visual source you selected to carry into the next lesson?

content.text: Introduce the lesson by showing students an image of Korean celadon pottery.
Turn and Talk
Use this brief routine to connect students’ recent work on Tree-ear’s observation skills to today’s research work with images.
Say:

In the previous lesson, we tracked how Tree-ear learns by watching carefully before he can make anything on his own. Today, we are going to use that same habit with visual sources by asking what an image shows, what it highlights, and what it leaves out. This matters because strong readers and researchers gather evidence from more than words.
Say these Directions:
Turn and talk to respond to the following question.
When you look at this image first, what do you notice right away, and what might that first detail make a viewer think about the pottery?

I notice that the vase is centered and the background is plain. That makes me focus on the smooth shape and decorations on the green glaze, so the image seems to present the pottery as valuable and important.
Teacher Tip

Use these visuals as specific sources connected to pottery making as craft and the celadon tradition that help students understand Tree-ear’s historical world. Remind students that one image does not stand for all artisan craft or Korean culture; instead, each image is a designed representation with its own source context, purpose, and limits.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say:
We will now move from quick noticing to a clear visual rhetoric routine we can use like researchers.
Students activate prior knowledge about apprenticeship and begin noticing that images are sources that make choices.
The teacher-maintained model topic for this research arc is
How do images communicate the value of Korean celadon craft?
Use this same model topic whenever you demonstrate research and media literacy moves in this arc.
Say:

Researchers do not treat images like decoration. We read them as sources by naming the choices the creator made. Today we will use four moves: composition, color and contrast, subject positioning, and absence.
Teach:

When I study this vase image, I start by naming what is literally there before I jump to meaning. I notice the vase is centered, brightly lit, and shown by itself, so the composition tells me the maker wants all my attention on the object. Then I ask what is missing, and I notice there are no people, tools, or workshop details, which means the image does not show the labor behind the piece. That helps me make a claim: this image argues that celadon pottery should be viewed as precious art.
Teacher Model: Visual Rhetoric Notes
Composition:
The vase is centered and fills most of the frame.
Color and contrast:
The carefully decorated green glaze stands out against a dark background.
Subject positioning:
The object is treated like the main subject, not like an everyday dish.
Absence:
No potter, tools, or workshop is shown.
Claim:
The image presents celadon as highly valued art, but it omits the effort and apprenticeship behind it.
Ask:
Which of the four visual rhetoric moves helps you go beyond saying “I see a pot,” and why?

The move about absence helps me most because it pushes me to notice what is not shown. That helps me understand that the image honors the finished object but leaves out the process and the people who made it.
Support students in using precise language to move from literal observation to evidence-based interpretation of a visual source.
Allow students to name first observations in a shared home language before restating them in English with a partner.
Invite students to connect this image-reading habit to how they already read photographs, videos, or social media images outside school.
Prompt students to separate observation from interpretation by asking, “What do you see first? What makes you say that?”
Encourage students to use the words
composition
and
omit
in complete sentences rather than as single-word labels.
You said, “The pot is in the middle” — we can explain that by saying: “The composition centers the vase.”
“That idea connects to absence because the image omits the potter and the workshop.”
Generative Oral/Language Supports:
The image includes ___, which makes the viewer notice ___.
The creator emphasizes ___ by ___.
The image omits ___, so it does not show ___.
If students only list details without explaining meaning → Prompt: “Choose one detail and finish this sentence: This detail suggests ___ because ___.”
If students confuse what is in the image with what they already know from the novel → Prompt: “Point to the part of the image that gave you that idea. Then add what you know from reading.”
Student names one exact visual detail before offering an interpretation.
Student uses a source-analysis verb, such as
emphasizes
or
omits
, to explain meaning.
Check for Understanding (RI.6.7)
Name one visual choice in the model image, and explain what it may communicate about celadon craft.
Connection to Today's Learning
Say
Now you are ready to apply the same four moves to additional sources and compare what images add to your understanding of craft.

content.text: Students now practice analyzing visual rhetoric in source material. Provide them with an image or allow them to choose one visual source from the visual source set from Lesson 42, the images in “Korean Ceramics of the Goryeo Period,” and/or teacher-selected images on celadon pottery and craft.
Say these Directions:

Work with your partner to analyze one of the craft images using the Media Literacy Image Analysis organizer. Record exact details from the image, and then explain what those details suggest about skill, culture, or value. Finally, add one note about how the image adds to what we have already learned from
A Single Shard
about observation, practice, or apprenticeship.
UPDATED PDF LINK:
https://drive.google.com/file/d/1f1Iagm46eZ769f6i6ejKX-dcsuuuQLC0/view?usp=sharing
Ask:
Which details does the image include and emphasize? What connections can you make to what you already know about observation, practice, or apprenticeship from reading
A Single Shard
Detail from the Image
Analysis of Detail
The potter’s hands are large in the frame.
The image emphasizes careful hand control. It helps me picture the physical skill behind the kind of work Tree-ear watches Min do.
Wet clay is being shaped in motion.
Making pottery takes steady practice, not speed. It adds a process detail that words alone may not fully show.
Tools and unfinished pieces are nearby.
Craft happens through repeated steps. It supports the idea that learning is gradual and refined over time.
Ask:
What does the image omit, and why does that omission matter?

The image omits the wider workshop and any teacher or apprentice relationship. That matters because it shows the action of making, but it does not fully show how knowledge is passed from one person to another.
Purpose: Support students in explaining how a visual source contributes information that deepens or changes understanding from reading.
Invite students to connect the image-reading process to how they already interpret visuals in games, videos, family photos, or online media.
Validate multiple pathways into the task by allowing a student to sketch and label the emphasized part of the image before writing a full sentence.
Prompt students to ground every interpretation in a specific visible detail before comparing it to the novel.
Encourage students to use temporal or process language when describing making:
first, during, while, after, from that point forward.
You said, “This shows work” — we can explain that by saying: “The image makes the process of the craft visible.”
You said, “The tools matter” — we can explain that by saying: “The source emphasizes the repeated steps needed to refine a piece.”
Generative Oral/Language Supports:
This image adds to my understanding because it shows ___.
Compared with the scene where Tree-ear observes Min, this image makes ___ easier to picture.
The source omits ___, so a viewer might not understand ___.
If students retell the novel instead of analyzing the image → Prompt: “Return to the source, and name one visible detail before connecting it to Tree-ear’s experience.”
If students make a broad claim about the image without precision → Prompt: “Be more specific. What tradition, object, or process in this image are you describing?”
Student cites one exact visual detail and explains what it suggests.
Student explains how the image adds information to prior reading rather than repeating the same idea.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with
moving from detail to interpretation:
Offer the frame: “The image shows ___, which suggests ___ because ___.”
connecting image evidence to prior reading:
Prompt students to finish: “Compared with the part where Tree-ear ___, this image helps me see ___.”
Ready for extension

Ask students to compare two images and explain which one better communicates the value of craft. Ask students to identify how a museum-style image and a process image make different arguments about the same craft tradition.
Learning in Action B: Select a Visual Source to Carry Forward (W.6.8)
(15 minutes)
Quickwrite

Students now choose one visual source to carry into the next lesson. They should review the visual source set from Lesson 42, the images in “Korean Ceramics of the Goryeo Period,” and any teacher-selected images to make their selection.
Say these Directions:

Choose one visual source connected to Korean art, pottery, or craft traditions that you want to study more closely in the next lesson. In 2–3 sentences, identify what the image includes, what it seems to emphasize or omit, and why it is a useful source for your research notes.
Ask:
Which visual source did you choose, and why is it worth carrying forward into the next lesson?

I chose the image of the potter’s hands shaping clay. It is useful because it emphasizes the careful process of making, not just the finished object. I want to carry it forward because it helps show how skill is built through repeated practice, which connects to Tree-ear’s apprenticeship.
Ask:
What is one note you will want to remember when you return to this image in the next lesson?

I want to remember that the close-up view makes the hands seem more important than the person’s face. That choice may be arguing that craft skill is developed through hours of practice and repeated movement.
Purpose: Support students in selecting a relevant visual source and recording clear notes they can use later without copying vague or unsupported claims.
Allow students to orally rehearse their note in a shared home language and then restate it in English with a partner.
Encourage students to use familiar image-reading habits from daily life as a strength when deciding what is emphasized.
You said, “I picked the hands one” — we can say: “I selected the close-up process image because it highlights skilled hand movement.”
You said, “It helps with my project” — we can say: “This source is relevant because it shows how craftsmanship develops through practice.”
Generative Oral/Language Supports:
I selected this source because it shows ___.
This image is relevant to my research because ___.
One note I need to carry forward is ___.
If students choose an image but cannot explain relevance → Prompt: “Which unit idea does this image help you understand better: skill, heritage, mentorship, or value?”
If students write a claim without evidence from the image → Prompt: “Add the exact detail in the image that led you to that idea.”
Student names a specific image and explains why it is relevant to the research focus.
Student records one reusable note grounded in a visible detail rather than a general opinion.
Pulse Check (RI.6.7)
Which response is the best example of a strong visual source analysis statement?
A. This picture is pretty, so it is a good source.
Incorrect: This response gives an opinion but does not analyze a visual choice or explain what information the image adds.
B. The image has pottery in it, and pottery is important in the book.
Incorrect: This notices the topic, but it does not explain how the image’s details communicate meaning.
C. The image centers the unfinished bowl and the potter’s hands, so it highlights the process of making and helps me understand the practice behind the finished art.
Correct: This response identifies a visual choice, explains what it emphasizes, and tells how the image adds understanding.
D. The image was taken a long time ago, so it must show exactly what Tree-ear saw.
Incorrect: This assumes accuracy without source evaluation and ignores that images are designed representations.
Situation
Try this
Struggling with
choosing a relevant image:
Narrow choices by asking students to pick the image that best matches one unit idea: apprenticeship, process, or finished art.
writing a clear source note:
Provide the frame: “I selected this source because it emphasizes ___ through ___.”
written output:
Allow students to record their note orally and then copy one sentence into their journal or Student Edition.
Ready for extension

Ask students to rank two possible images and justify which one is the stronger research source. Ask students to add one question they still have about the image that would require another source to answer.
Learning in Action A: Read Two Craft Images Closely (RI.6.7)
Students integrate information from multiple sources to explain how visual media add to their understanding of skill, craft, and apprenticeship.
Learning in Action B: Select a Visual Source to Carry Forward (W.6.8)
Students choose one relevant image and record source notes they will use in the next lesson.
Quick Write
Students answer both reflection prompts to generate formative data and prepare for the next research lesson.
Say these Directions:
Use your notes from today to answer both reflection prompts. Be specific about one visual choice you noticed and one next step you will take as a researcher.
Ask:
What new information did you learn today from a visual source that words alone did not make as clear?

I learned that a visual source can make the physical process of pottery easier to picture. The close-up of the potter’s hands and the wet clay showed how much control and repetition the work takes, which helped me understand skill-building in a more concrete way.
Ask:
What is your next step for the visual source you selected to carry into the next lesson?
My next step is to return to the same image and annotate exactly what it emphasizes and omits. I also want to record the source title so I can use the image responsibly in my notes.
Students reflect on what visual evidence helped them learn and what next step they will take as researchers.
Review your selected visual source note from today. Be ready to return to that same source in the next lesson and add fuller annotations.

standards.description: Integrate information presented in different media or formats (e.g., visually, quantitatively) as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.

Gather relevant information from multiple print and digital sources; assess the credibility of each source; and quote or paraphrase the data and conclusions of others while avoiding plagiarism and providing basic bibliographic information for sources.
Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.

Come to discussions prepared, having read or studied required material; explicitly draw on that preparation by referring to evidence on the topic, text, or issue to probe and reflect on ideas under discussion.
Follow rules for collegial discussions, set specific goals and deadlines, and define individual roles as needed.
Pose and respond to specific questions with elaboration and detail by making comments that contribute to the topic, text, or issue under discussion.
Review the key ideas expressed and demonstrate understanding of multiple perspectives through reflection and paraphrasing.

Contribute to class, group, and partner discussions by following turn‐taking rules, asking relevant questions, affirming others, adding relevant information and evidence, paraphrasing key ideas, building on responses, and providing useful feedback.
Engage in conversational exchanges and express ideas on familiar topics by asking and answering yes‐no and wh‐ questions and responding using simple phrases.
